desc:
Given a non-negative integer n, return the number of zeros at the end of the decimal representation of n! (that is, 1 * 2 * ... * n, with 0! = 1).

The factorial itself is astronomically large for big n, so you cannot compute it directly.

n = 5   -> 5! = 120        -> 1
n = 10  -> 10! = 3628800   -> 2
n = 25  -> 25! ends in 6 zeros
hints: Each trailing zero comes from one factor of 10 in the product.
10 = 2 * 5, and there are always more factors of 2 than factors of 5 in n!, so count the 5s.
Multiples of 25 contribute two 5s, multiples of 125 three, and so on. Sum n//5 + n//25 + n//125 + ....
editorial: The number of trailing zeros equals the exponent of 10 in n!, which is the smaller of the exponents of 2 and 5. Factors of 2 are far more plentiful, so the exponent of 5 decides.

Every multiple of 5 up to n contributes at least one 5: there are n // 5 of them. Every multiple of 25 contributes an extra one: n // 25 more, then n // 125, and so on. The terms shrink geometrically, so the loop runs about log5 n times.
